solution.concept_anchor: Maratha confederacy formation timeline vs Shivaji
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students associate Shivaji's administrative genius with the confederacy's creation, conflating his centralised kingdom with a later, structurally distinct political arrangement.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Shivaji established a centralised kingdom, not a confederacy — the confederacy emerged after his death under Peshwa leadership.
Eliminate (c): The Battle of Plassey (1757) concerns British power in Bengal, not Maratha confederacy formation.
Eliminate (d): The Treaty of Purandar (1776) relates to the First Anglo-Maratha War, not the confederacy's institutional origins.
Confirm (b): The Battle of Khed (1707) and Balaji Vishwanath's subsequent role mark the institutional consolidation of the confederacy.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: A student with surface knowledge links 'Maratha power' with Shivaji and assumes the confederacy is his creation. In reality, Shivaji's system was highly centralised with the Chhatrapati at its apex. The confederacy — a looser arrangement of semi-autonomous chiefs under nominal Chhatrapati sovereignty — crystallised only after Shivaji's death, with the Battle of Khed (1707) and Balaji Vishwanath's political manoeuvring being the key institutional milestones.
solution.final_explanation:
The Maratha polity underwent a fundamental structural transformation between Shivaji's reign and the early 18th century. Shivaji built a tightly centralised state with himself as Chhatrapati and the Ashta Pradhan serving as an advisory council subordinate to royal authority. The confederacy, by contrast, was a loose association of powerful chiefs who acknowledged the Chhatrapati's nominal suzerainty while exercising near-sovereign authority in their own territories.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Shivaji's system was centralised, not confederate. The confederacy emerged posthumously.
• Option (b) — Correct: The Battle of Khed (1707), in which Balaji Vishwanath helped Shahu defeat Tarabai, was the pivotal military event after which the Peshwa's role as the de facto organiser of the confederacy was institutionalised.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Battle of Plassey (1757) is unrelated to Maratha institutional history.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Treaty of Purandar (1776) pertains to the First Anglo-Maratha War.

Value Addition:
• Balaji Vishwanath (first Peshwa of the hereditary line) secured the release of Shahu from Mughal captivity, earning tremendous political capital.
• The Chhatrapati at Satara became increasingly ceremonial after the 1720s.
• The confederacy's decentralised design was both its strength (flexibility) and its fatal weakness (lack of unified command).

solution.concept_anchor: Peshwa contributions — territorial vs administrative vs decline

statement_analysis.statement: Baji Rao I was primarily responsible for the spectacular territorial expansion of the Maratha Confederacy into Gujarat, Malwa, and the northern plains.
statement_analysis.reason: Baji Rao I (1720–1740) led military campaigns that extended Maratha influence into Gujarat, Malwa, Bundelkhand, and conducted the famous raid on Delhi in 1737, making him the principal architect of territorial expansion.

statement_analysis.statement: Balaji Baji Rao (Nana Saheb) was Peshwa during the Third Battle of Panipat and is primarily associated with the administrative and fiscal consolidation of the early confederacy.
statement_analysis.reason: While Balaji Baji Rao (Nana Saheb) was indeed Peshwa during the Third Battle of Panipat (1761), the administrative and fiscal consolidation of the early confederacy is primarily credited to Balaji Vishwanath (the first hereditary Peshwa), not to Nana Saheb, who presided over the confederacy's overextension and the catastrophic Panipat defeat.

statement_analysis.statement: Balaji Vishwanath's most significant contribution was transforming the Peshwa from a ministerial post into the hereditary de facto head of the confederacy.
statement_analysis.reason: Balaji Vishwanath secured hereditary rights to the Peshwaship, effectively converting what had been an appointed royal minister into a dynastic office that controlled the confederacy's real power.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because students who know Nana Saheb was Peshwa during Panipat may incorrectly conflate administrative credit with administrative achievement, assuming the most 'famous' Peshwa of an era also performed the most administrative work.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: Baji Rao I's northern campaigns including the Delhi raid of 1737 are well-established — Statement 1 is correct.

Examine Statement 2 carefully: Balaji Baji Rao was Peshwa during Panipat (true), but 'administrative consolidation of the early confederacy' belongs to Balaji Vishwanath, not Nana Saheb — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Confirm Statement 3: Balaji Vishwanath's securing of hereditary Peshwaship is foundational — Statement 3 is correct.
Correct and incorrect pattern is 1 and 3 — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits entity-swap across Peshwas. Students memorise names but swap their contributions. Balaji Vishwanath = institutional founder; Baji Rao I = territorial expander; Balaji Baji Rao (Nana Saheb) = presided over Panipat. The statement about Nana Saheb credits him with early consolidation — a role that belongs to his grandfather Balaji Vishwanath. A partially prepared student who knows Nana Saheb's association with Panipat may miss the false attribution of 'administrative consolidation.'
solution.final_explanation:
The Peshwa office evolved through three distinct phases: institutional founding (Balaji Vishwanath), territorial expansion (Baji Rao I), and overextension leading to decline (Balaji Baji Rao / Nana Saheb).

• Statement 1 — Correct: Baji Rao I's campaigns in Gujarat, Malwa, Bundelkhand, and the 1737 Delhi raid define the confederacy's expansionary peak. He is correctly identified with territorial growth.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The administrative consolidation of the early confederacy belongs to Balaji Vishwanath, the first hereditary Peshwa. Nana Saheb is primarily associated with the period of overextension and the catastrophic defeat at Panipat (1761), not with early administrative reform.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Balaji Vishwanath's securing of the hereditary Peshwaship converted a royal appointment into a dynastic office — the most consequential structural change in the confederacy's governance.

Value Addition:
• Baji Rao I is considered by many historians as the greatest of the Peshwas militarily — he never lost a battle.
• After Panipat, the effective revival fell to Madhavrao I, not to any of the older Peshwa line.
• The hereditary Peshwaship created its own succession crises, which the British later exploited systematically.

solution.concept_anchor: Geographic domains of five Maratha chief houses

statement_analysis.statement: The Scindias (Shindes) were headquartered at Gwalior and were the most powerful Maratha house in northern India by the late 18th century.
statement_analysis.reason: The Scindias were indeed based at Gwalior and, under Mahadaji Scindia, became the dominant Maratha power in northern India, exercising a protectorate over the Mughal Emperor.

statement_analysis.statement: The Holkars were based at Baroda and controlled territories in Gujarat, while the Gaekwads were headquartered at Indore.
statement_analysis.reason: This statement swaps the two houses — the Holkars were based at Indore (controlling Malwa), while the Gaekwads were based at Baroda (controlling Gujarat). The statement reverses their geographic seats.

statement_analysis.statement: The Bhonsles of Nagpur expanded Maratha influence into Bengal, Orissa, and Central India, representing the easternmost reach of the confederacy.
statement_analysis.reason: Raghuji Bhonsle I led expeditions into Bengal and Orissa, making the Nagpur Bhonsles the principal agents of Maratha expansion in eastern and central India.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) pointing to Statement 3 is a distractor because students who associate 'Bhonsle' primarily with Shivaji's clan in Satara may doubt that the Nagpur Bhonsles had such an independent eastern expansion.
elimination_logic: Check Statement 1: Scindias at Gwalior, dominant in northern India under Mahadaji — this is well-established and correct; Statement 1 is NOT the incorrect one.
Check Statement 2: 'Holkars at Baroda, Gaekwads at Indore' — this is a direct reversal; Holkars = Indore, Gaekwads = Baroda. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Check Statement 3: Nagpur Bhonsles' expansion into Bengal and Orissa under Raghuji I is historically accurate — Statement 3 is correct.
The question asks which is NOT correct — only Statement 2 qualifies; select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap between Holkars and Gaekwads is a classic UPSC-style trap. Both are associated with western India but in different states — Holkars with Malwa/Indore and Gaekwads with Gujarat/Baroda. Students who have memorised the five houses without anchoring each to its precise location will likely accept Statement 2 as plausible or fail to detect the swap. The reversed pairing sounds structurally credible because both Baroda and Indore are 'western' cities.
solution.final_explanation:
The five principal houses of the Maratha Confederacy each controlled distinct geographic zones: Peshwas (Pune/Deccan), Bhonsles (Nagpur/Central-East India), Scindias (Gwalior/North India), Holkars (Indore/Malwa), and Gaekwads (Baroda/Gujarat).

• Statement 1 — Correct: Scindias were headquartered at Gwalior. Under Mahadaji Scindia, they became the most formidable Maratha presence in northern India and exercised a protectorate over the Mughal court.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The statement swaps Holkars and Gaekwads. Holkars = Indore (Malwa region); Gaekwads = Baroda (Gujarat). This is the statement that is NOT correct.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Raghuji Bhonsle I of Nagpur conducted multiple campaigns into Bengal and Orissa, making the Nagpur branch the easternmost expansionist force of the confederacy.

Value Addition:
• The Gaekwads of Baroda signed an early subsidiary alliance and largely avoided direct confrontation with the British in the Third Anglo-Maratha War.
• Holkars and Scindias had persistent rivalry — the Battle of Ujjain (1728) reflects early inter-house tensions.
• The Nagpur Bhonsles are distinct from the Satara Bhonsles (Shivaji's direct line) — a common point of confusion.

solution.concept_anchor: Chauth vs Sardeshmukhi — rates, nature, and basis

statement_analysis.statement: Chauth was levied at one-quarter of the assessed revenue of a territory as a protection payment to avoid Maratha raids.
statement_analysis.reason: Chauth (literally 'one-fourth') was collected at 25% of a region's assessed revenue and functioned as a protection tax — territories paying it were theoretically immune from Maratha plunder.

statement_analysis.statement: Sardeshmukhi was an additional levy of one-tenth of revenue, claimed on the basis of the Maratha king's hereditary right as the senior headman (Sardeshmukh) of Maharashtra.
statement_analysis.reason: Sardeshmukhi (10% of revenue) rested on the claim that the Chhatrapati was the hereditary Sardeshmukh — senior headman — of all Maharashtra, giving a traditional legitimacy to the levy distinct from Chauth's protective rationale.

statement_analysis.statement: Both Chauth and Sardeshmukhi were forms of direct land revenue and were incorporated into the regular Mughal revenue assessment system.
statement_analysis.reason: Neither levy was part of the Mughal revenue system — they were parallel extractions imposed by the Marathas on territories they did not directly govern, and were not classified as regular land revenue under any Mughal administrative framework.

statement_analysis.statement: The Peshwa and individual confederacy chiefs sometimes competed for the right to collect Chauth from the same territories, reflecting the confederacy's lack of a unified fiscal system.
statement_analysis.reason: The confederacy's decentralised structure meant that multiple Maratha chiefs claimed and collected Chauth from overlapping zones, creating jurisdictional disputes that weakened the fiscal coherence of the confederacy.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' tempts students who correctly identify Statement 3 as false but are uncertain whether the Peshwa-vs-chiefs fiscal rivalry (Statement 4) is a documented fact or an inference.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 — Correct: Chauth = 1/4 of revenue as protection payment — well-established definition.
Statement 2 — Correct: Sardeshmukhi = 1/10 of revenue, based on hereditary Sardeshmukh claim — correctly stated.
Statement 3 — Incorrect: These were NOT Mughal revenue categories; they were parallel Maratha extractions outside the Mughal fiscal framework.
Statement 4 — Correct: Jurisdictional overlaps in Chauth collection among confederacy chiefs are historically documented — select 'Only three' which maps to option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
Chauth and Sardeshmukhi were the twin fiscal instruments through which the Marathas extracted revenue from territories under suzerainty without direct governance. Chauth (25% of assessed revenue) was a protection levy; Sardeshmukhi (10%) was a claim rooted in the Chhatrapati's status as hereditary senior headman of Maharashtra. Statement 3 is the false one — these were emphatically not part of the Mughal land revenue system but parallel Maratha impositions.

Value Addition:
• Together, Chauth and Sardeshmukhi amounted to 35% of a region's assessed revenue — a substantial fiscal burden on territories under Maratha suzerainty.
• Shivaji used these instruments to finance his campaigns without direct annexation, allowing flexible expansion.
• Under the confederacy, the fragmented collection of Chauth by multiple chiefs reduced fiscal efficiency and often antagonised potential regional allies.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because it correctly places Deogaon with the Bhonsle but swaps Surji-Anjangaon (Scindia) and Bassein (Peshwa), which students who have partial recall of the Second Anglo-Maratha War may not detect.
elimination_logic: Anchor A: Treaty of Bassein (1802) is unambiguously associated with Peshwa Baji Rao II — this eliminates options placing Bassein with any other chief.
Anchor B: Treaty of Deogaon (1803) is associated with Bhonsle of Nagpur — confirmed by Arthur Wellesley's campaign in eastern India.
Anchor C: Treaty of Surji-Anjangaon (1803) was signed by Daulat Rao Scindia — eliminates options placing it with Holkar or Bhonsle.
Anchor D: Treaty of Rajpurghat (1806) concluded the British campaign against Holkar after Yashwantrao Holkar's resistance — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits the entity-swap between Scindia and Holkar. Students who know Deogaon (Bhonsle) and Bassein (Peshwa) as anchors may then guess incorrectly between Surji-Anjangaon and Rajpurghat, swapping which treaty was signed by Scindias versus Holkars. The proximity of both the Second and Third Anglo-Maratha War treaties in time and name creates additional confusion.
solution.final_explanation:
The Anglo-Maratha Wars produced a cascade of treaties, each with a specific signatory from the confederacy. Tracking which chief signed which treaty is a high-yield factual cluster for UPSC.

Correct matches:
• A → 3 (Bassein/Peshwa): Treaty of Bassein (1802) was signed by Peshwa Baji Rao II accepting Subsidiary Alliance — the proximate cause of the Second Anglo-Maratha War.
• B → 1 (Deogaon/Bhonsle): Treaty of Deogaon (1803) ended the British campaign against Raghuji Bhonsle II of Nagpur.
• C → 4 (Surji-Anjangaon/Scindia): Treaty of Surji-Anjangaon (1803) was signed by Daulat Rao Scindia after defeats at Assaye and Laswari.
• D → 2 (Rajpurghat/Holkar): Treaty of Rajpurghat (1806) concluded hostilities with Yashwantrao Holkar.

Value Addition:
• Arthur Wellesley (later Duke of Wellington) gained his military reputation at the Battle of Assaye against Scindia.
• The Treaty of Bassein is considered the single most consequential Anglo-Maratha agreement — it effectively ended Maratha sovereign independence.
• Holkars were the last confederacy house to formally engage the British and the last to accept the Subsidiary Alliance (1818).

solution.concept_anchor: Third Battle of Panipat — multi-causal defeat analysis
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) tempts students who know both A and R are factually true but fail to critically examine whether R is the actual explanation for A rather than merely a correlated factor.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. The Marathas were defeated at the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) against Ahmad Shah Durrani's forces.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. The Holkars did not participate in the Panipat campaign, and the Nizam declined to ally with the Marathas, both of which are documented historical facts.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — Not fully. While allied defections contributed, the defeat resulted from multiple compounding factors including logistical overstretch, supply disruption, and Afghan cavalry superiority. R identifies only one dimension and cannot be the sole or principal explanation of A.
Since both A and R are correct but R does NOT fully explain A in a causally sufficient manner, the answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits reversed-causation expectations. Students who correctly identify both A and R as factually true instinctively select (a), assuming that any true R must explain A. But UPSC specifically tests whether students can distinguish between correlation and causation. The Holkar non-participation and Nizam's absence were contributing factors but not the principal explanatory cause — the defeat involved logistical failure, supply line disruption, and military tactics. R is true but incomplete as a causal explanation of A.
solution.final_explanation:
The Third Battle of Panipat (1761) was one of the most consequential military events in Indian history. The Maratha forces under Vishwasrao and Bhau Saheb were decisively defeated by Ahmad Shah Durrani's Afghan coalition.

Assertion (A) analysis: Factually unambiguous — the Maratha defeat at Panipat in January 1761 is a core historical fact.

Reason (R) analysis: Also factually correct — Yashwantrao Holkar's forces did not participate meaningfully in the Panipat campaign, and the Nizam of Hyderabad aligned with the Afghan side rather than supporting the Marathas.

Causal relationship: R identifies real contributing factors but cannot causally explain A sufficiently. The defeat arose from multiple simultaneous failures: overextended supply lines, inability to receive provisions over winter, Afghan superiority in cavalry warfare, and the catastrophic decision to fight a pitched battle rather than use Maratha guerrilla strengths. Allied defections were symptomatic of broader diplomatic failure, not the sole cause.

Value Addition:
• The Marathas lost an estimated 28,000 soldiers and multiple commanders including Vishwasrao and Bhau Saheb at Panipat.
• The political recovery under Madhavrao I (Peshwa) after 1761 was remarkably swift — within a decade Maratha influence had returned to Delhi.
• Panipat (1761) was the third major battle on that historic field — preceded by the First (1526, Babur vs Ibrahim Lodi) and Second (1556, Akbar vs Hemu).

solution.concept_anchor: First Anglo-Maratha War — key events in sequence
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because students who know Salbai ended the war and Wadgaon was a British defeat may place them in plausible-sounding but wrong relative order.
elimination_logic: Anchor the start: British intervention in Peshwa succession (Raghoba dispute) preceded any military engagement — this is Event 1.
Convention of Wadgaon (1779): The British suffered a humiliating defeat forcing a convention — this occurred during the war, after intervention but before its resolution.
Treaty of Purandar (1776) preceded the Wadgaon Convention — it was an early British attempt to negotiate with the Marathas before full-scale war.
Treaty of Salbai (1782) ended the war — it must be last in the sequence, confirming order: Raghoba dispute → Purandar → Wadgaon → Salbai, making (c) correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap here involves placing the Treaty of Purandar and the Convention of Wadgaon in the wrong order. Students who know both events belong to the First Anglo-Maratha War period but cannot precisely recall which came first will often reverse them. Purandar (1776) was an early peace attempt that collapsed; Wadgaon (1779) was the battlefield defeat that forced a humiliating convention on the British — knowing this causal chain resolves the sequence.
solution.final_explanation:
The First Anglo-Maratha War (1775–1782) unfolded through a sequence of diplomatic and military events rooted in the Peshwa succession dispute.

Correct chronological order:
1. British intervention in Raghoba's (Raghunathrao's) succession claim: The British backed Raghoba as a client Peshwa — this was the war's trigger.
2. Treaty of Purandar (1776): An early, ultimately ineffective agreement that the Marathas repudiated.
3. Convention of Wadgaon (1779): British forces suffered defeat and were compelled to sign a humiliating convention — the most significant British military reversal of the war.
4. Treaty of Salbai (1782): Ended the war on a status quo ante basis, giving the British time to recover and consolidate.

Why wrong options fail: Options placing Wadgaon before Purandar, or Salbai before Wadgaon, misread the causal chain — the war escalated from diplomacy to defeat to eventual treaty.

Value Addition:
• The Convention of Wadgaon is notable as one of the rare instances of a British military capitulation in India.
• The Treaty of Salbai is strategically significant because it gave the British two decades to consolidate before the Second Anglo-Maratha War.
• Mahadaji Scindia played a key mediating role in negotiating the Treaty of Salbai.

solution.concept_anchor: Treaty of Bassein — confederacy-wide implications of bilateral agreement
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students correctly understand Bassein was a Subsidiary Alliance agreement and may select it without recognising that the question specifically probes the treaty's confederacy-wide implications beyond the bilateral dimension.
elimination_logic: Identify the core question: the scenario asks which principle explains why a bilateral treaty between the British and Peshwa provoked all other Maratha chiefs — this requires understanding Bassein's confederacy-wide effect.

Eliminate (a): While Bassein was indeed a Subsidiary Alliance, identifying it as such does not explain why it triggered inter-Maratha conflict — the principle of confederacy sovereignty is the operative concept.
Eliminate (b): Doctrine of Lapse relates to adoption rights and succession, not to treaty obligations — irrelevant here.
Eliminate (d): The scenario does not involve a war of expansion or annexation at this stage — 'Forward Policy' is a 19th-century concept associated with Lord Dalhousie.

Confirm (c): The Peshwa's acceptance of British paramountcy through Bassein effectively subordinated the entire confederacy's foreign policy, triggering Scindia and Bhonsle resistance — this is the correct principle.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap works here because students correctly identify Bassein as a Subsidiary Alliance (true) but assume that label is sufficient to answer the question. The question probes a deeper principle — that a bilateral agreement between the British and the titular head of the confederacy (Peshwa) was interpreted by other chiefs as a surrender of the entire confederacy's sovereignty, not merely a Peshwa-British arrangement. This distinction between bilateral mechanics and confederacy-wide implications is what UPSC tests.
solution.final_explanation:
The Treaty of Bassein (1802) was signed by Peshwa Baji Rao II following his defeat by Yashwantrao Holkar at the Battle of Hadapsar and his flight to British protection at Bassein. The treaty accepted the terms of the Subsidiary Alliance — British troops stationed in Peshwa territories, Maratha foreign policy controlled by the British, and territorial concessions.

Why this triggered the Second Anglo-Maratha War:
Although Bassein was technically a bilateral treaty between the British and the Peshwa, the Peshwa held nominal sovereignty over the entire confederacy. His acceptance of British paramountcy was perceived by Scindias and Bhonsles not as a personal arrangement but as a unilateral surrender of confederacy sovereignty. This violated the implicit compact among confederacy chiefs that no single house could subordinate the confederacy's collective foreign policy.

• Option (a) — Insufficient: Labels the treaty correctly but doesn't explain the confederacy-wide implication.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Doctrine of Lapse is unrelated.
• Option (c) — Correct: The bilateral agreement effectively imposed British paramountcy on the entire confederacy, triggering collective resistance.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Forward Policy is a later, distinct concept.

Value Addition:
• Bassein is often called the 'death warrant' of the Maratha Confederacy.
• Lord Wellesley used Bassein to justify his subsequent campaigns against Scindias and Bhonsles as 'resisting the legitimate Peshwa's treaty.'.
• The treaty gave the British a legal pretext to intervene anywhere in the confederacy's sphere.

formatted_presentation.display_text:
Following his defeat in battle and flight to the British at Bassein, a prominent Maratha leader signed a comprehensive agreement with the British East India Company in 1802. The agreement required him to permanently station British troops within his territories at his own expense, surrender control over his relations with external powers, and make territorial concessions. When news of this agreement reached other powerful houses within the same political confederation, they immediately began military preparations against both the signatory and the British, viewing the agreement as a betrayal of their collective political independence.

(b) The Doctrine of Lapse applied to the signatory's territories, giving the British grounds to annex the entire confederacy.

solution.concept_anchor: Maratha relations with northern Indian powers — alliances vs antagonism
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because students who associate Sikhs primarily with Maratha cooperation (both being Hindu powers against the Mughals) may overlook that Maratha-Sikh relations were tactically adversarial rather than consistently cooperative.
elimination_logic: Identify the category: three of the four options describe powers with which the Marathas had at least some tactical or tributary alliance relationship.
Rajput states: Marathas extracted tribute from Rajput states but also periodically used them as buffer allies — tactical alliance existed.
Mughal Emperor (Shah Alam II): Mahadaji Scindia exercised a formal protectorate over the Mughal Emperor — a cooperation/subordination relationship existed.
Jat rulers: Marathas cooperated with Jat rulers around the Delhi-Doab region on specific campaigns — tactical alliances documented.

Eliminate (b): Sikh power under Ranjit Singh actively resisted Maratha expansion in the Punjab — there was no sustained tactical alliance, making Sikhs the odd one out in the context of 'powers with whom Marathas had cooperative or tributary arrangements.'
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap assumes students will apply the logic 'both Marathas and Sikhs were anti-Mughal, therefore they allied.' This is an oversimplification. While both powers were non-Muslim, their geographic and political interests in the Punjab-Doab region were often competitive. Students who read 'Maratha alliances with northern powers' too broadly will include Sikhs, missing the fact that Sikh-Maratha relations were more rivalrous than cooperative in the 18th century.
solution.final_explanation:
Maratha expansion into northern India created complex relationships — sometimes tributary, sometimes cooperative — with the region's political powers.

• Option (a) — Rajput states: Marathas extracted tribute from Rajput chiefs like those of Jaipur and Jodhpur, but also periodically cooperated with them against common threats. A tribute-extraction relationship constitutes a form of Maratha overlordship.
• Option (b) — Sikh rulers under Ranjit Singh: This is the ODD ONE OUT. Maratha expansion into the Punjab was actively resisted by Sikh power. There was no sustained tributary or cooperative alliance between the Marathas and Sikhs — their interests in the Punjab-Doab region were frequently adversarial.
• Option (c) — Jat rulers (Bharatpur): Marathas and Jats had tactical cooperation around Delhi — the Jat ruler Suraj Mal had interactions with Maratha commanders during the pre-Panipat period.
• Option (d) — Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II: Mahadaji Scindia exercised a formal protectorate over the Mughal court after 1771 — the most explicit cooperative arrangement between the Marathas and a northern power.

Value Addition:
• Mahadaji Scindia's control over Shah Alam II made the Marathas the de facto power behind the Mughal throne briefly in the 1780s.
• Maratha-Rajput relations were economically exploitative — the 'alliance' was really coercive suzerainty.
• The failure to forge a Hindu coalition including Sikhs and Rajputs weakened Maratha resistance to British expansion.

solution.concept_anchor: Mahadaji Scindia vs Daulat Rao Scindia — peak of Scindia power

statement_analysis.statement: Mahadaji Scindia exercised a protectorate over the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II and represented the zenith of Scindia political and military power in northern India.
statement_analysis.reason: Mahadaji Scindia (d. 1794) rehabilitated Maratha prestige after Panipat, restored Shah Alam II to Delhi under Maratha protection, and became the most powerful political actor in northern India in the 1780s — this represents the Scindia peak, not any later period.

statement_analysis.statement: Daulat Rao Scindia, who succeeded Mahadaji, maintained and further extended this northern Indian dominance until the Second Anglo-Maratha War secured Scindia supremacy in the region.
statement_analysis.reason: Daulat Rao Scindia did not maintain the Mahadaji-era dominance — his reign was marked by military defeats at Assaye and Laswari and the loss of northern Indian territories under the Treaty of Surji-Anjangaon (1803). The Second Anglo-Maratha War decisively diminished, not extended, Scindia power.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) tempts students who know Daulat Rao was Mahadaji's successor and assume a hereditary house would maintain its predecessor's dominance, missing the catastrophic impact of the Second Anglo-Maratha War.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Mahadaji Scindia's protectorate over Shah Alam II and his peak power in northern India (1770s–1794) is historically well-established — Statement 1 is correct.

Verify Statement 2: Daulat Rao Scindia faced defeats at Assaye (1803) and under Treaty of Surji-Anjangaon lost major northern territories — this directly contradicts the claim of 'maintained and further extended dominance' — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Since Statement 1 is correct and Statement 2 is incorrect, the answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap exploits the easy assumption that a political dynasty's power trajectory is continuous. Students who know Mahadaji = zenith of Scindia power but forget that Daulat Rao's tenure saw sharp decline will incorrectly mark Statement 2 as plausible. The trap is reinforced by the phrase 'Second Anglo-Maratha War secured Scindia supremacy' — in reality, the Second Anglo-Maratha War did the opposite.
solution.final_explanation:
Mahadaji Scindia (Madhoji Shinde) is the pivotal figure of late 18th-century northern Indian politics. After surviving Panipat (1761), he rebuilt Scindia military power using European-trained infantry under commanders like De Boigne. His protectorate over the weakened Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II gave him symbolic control over the imperial court at Delhi — the political apex of Scindia, and indeed Maratha, power.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Shah Alam II protectorate and northern Indian dominance are precisely associated with Mahadaji (d. 1794) — this is the confirmed zenith.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Daulat Rao Scindia's period (post-1794) was one of decline. His defeats at Assaye (1803) by Arthur Wellesley and at Laswari by Lake, followed by the Treaty of Surji-Anjangaon, dismantled northern Scindia dominance. The Second Anglo-Maratha War shrank, not extended, Scindia power.

Value Addition:
• De Boigne and later Perron trained the Scindia forces as a formidable European-style army — yet it proved insufficient against the British in 1803.
• Mahadaji is sometimes called the 'last great Maratha' — his death in 1794 marked the beginning of confederacy disintegration.
• Daulat Rao Scindia later became a British subordinate under the Subsidiary Alliance framework.

solution.concept_anchor: Ashta Pradhan — function under Shivaji vs confederacy period
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because 'Peshwa's privy council' sounds administratively plausible for the confederacy period and students who know the Ashta Pradhan was diluted may over-interpret its role as having been re-created as a Peshwa-era institution.
elimination_logic: Recall the Ashta Pradhan: Shivaji created eight ministers (Ashta Pradhan) with specific functional portfolios — each was appointed by and accountable to the Chhatrapati.
Under the confederacy, the Peshwa absorbed most administrative functions — individual Ashta Pradhan members lost collective advisory power and became subordinate to Peshwa's office.
Eliminate (a): The Ashta Pradhan was NOT a constitutional cabinet in the modern sense — it had no legislative functions.
Eliminate (c) and (d): 'Privy council' and 'revenue collection board' misrepresent the original and confederacy-era roles.
Confirm (b): Under the confederacy, the Ashta Pradhan became a largely ceremonial body, with real power concentrated in the Peshwa's administration.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap works by implying the Ashta Pradhan retained its Shivaji-era functional significance under the confederacy. Students who have studied Shivaji's administration in detail know the Ashta Pradhan was an effective advisory-executive council. The trap is assuming it continued similarly under the confederacy — in reality, the Peshwa's centralisation rendered it ceremonial.
solution.final_explanation:
Shivaji's Ashta Pradhan (Eight Ministers) was a functional executive council with specific portfolios: Peshwa (prime minister), Amatya (finance), Sachiv (correspondence), Sumant (foreign affairs), Senapati (military), Pandit Rao (religious affairs), Nyayadhish (justice), and Mantri (intelligence). Each minister reported directly to the Chhatrapati.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Ashta Pradhan was an executive-advisory body, not a constitutional legislative cabinet.
• Option (b) — Correct: Under the confederacy, as the Peshwa's office absorbed executive functions, the Ashta Pradhan's collective role was progressively reduced to ceremonial status — individual office-holders continued but lacked the independent authority they had under Shivaji.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: 'Privy council' mischaracterises both its original role and its confederacy-era dilution.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Revenue collection was handled through the Chauth-Sardeshmukhi system and individual chiefs — not by the Ashta Pradhan as a body.

Value Addition:
• The Peshwa himself was originally one of eight Ashta Pradhan members — his rise to dominance is a story of one office eclipsing the entire council.
• The Amatya (finance minister) and Sachiv (record keeper) were the two posts most relevant to revenue administration.
• The Senapati (commander) position became less relevant as individual confederacy chiefs commanded their own armies.

solution.concept_anchor: Gaekwad non-participation in Third Anglo-Maratha War
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students who know the Peshwaship was abolished and Baji Rao II was pensioned at Bithur may conflate 'abolition' with 'death' or confuse the location of his pensioning.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Peshwa Baji Rao II's attack on the British Residency at Kirkee (Pune) is the documented triggering event of the Third Anglo-Maratha War — this pair is correctly matched.
Eliminate (b): Baji Rao II was pensioned at Bithur (near Kanpur), not at Satara — 'Satara' is a wrong geographic attribution; but the question asks for the CORRECTLY matched pair.
Eliminate (c): Holkar of Indore did engage British forces during the Third Anglo-Maratha War — this claim of non-participation would be incorrect.

Confirm (d): The Gaekwad of Baroda did NOT actively oppose the British in the Third Anglo-Maratha War — they had earlier aligned with British interests and were among the chiefs who 'survived' with their principality intact precisely because of their cooperative posture.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Gaekwad's non-participation in the Third Anglo-Maratha War is an explicit UPSC trap dimension from the key_dimensions. Students who know the Third Anglo-Maratha War involved 'the Marathas' may assume all five chief houses opposed the British simultaneously. In reality, the Gaekwads of Baroda had aligned with the British much earlier and did not actively resist — which is why Baroda survived as a princely state while the Peshwaship and other houses were dissolved.
solution.final_explanation:
The Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817–1818) was fought simultaneously on multiple fronts — against the Peshwa, the Bhonsle of Nagpur, and the Holkar of Indore.

• Option (a) — Correctly matched: The Peshwa Baji Rao II's attack on the British Residency at Kirkee (Pune) in November 1817 is the documented trigger of the war.
• Option (b) — Incorrectly matched: Baji Rao II was pensioned at Bithur near Kanpur, not at Satara. Satara was where a Chhatrapati was later installed as a British-managed figurehead.
• Option (c) — Incorrectly matched: Holkar of Indore did engage the British — Yashwantrao Holkar II fought before eventually submitting. The claim of non-participation is false.
• Option (d) — Correctly matched: The Gaekwad of Baroda had earlier cooperated with the British and did NOT actively oppose them in 1817–18. Baroda consequently survived as a princely state throughout British rule.

Value Addition:
• The abolition of the Peshwaship in 1818 ended the Maratha Confederacy as a political entity.
• Baji Rao II's adopted son, Nana Saheb Peshwa, later became a leader in the 1857 uprising — a direct consequence of the British pension arrangement at Bithur.
• The Gaekwad survival strategy — early accommodation with the British — contrasts sharply with the fate of the Peshwa and Bhonsle.

solution.concept_anchor: Hindu Pad Padshahi — aspiration vs formal policy
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students who have read about Baji Rao I's northern campaigns readily associate 'Hindu Pad Padshahi' with a fully articulated pan-Hindu political programme, missing the critical distinction between rhetorical aspiration and formal policy.
elimination_logic: Recall the concept: 'Hindu Pad Padshahi' translates broadly as 'Hindu political supremacy' — associated with Baji Rao I's vision for the confederacy's northern expansion.

Eliminate (b): Characterising it as a 'formal policy with defined constitutional structure' is an overreach — it was a political aspiration articulated by Baji Rao I, not an institutionalised programme.
Eliminate (c): The concept was not rejected by the Peshwas — Baji Rao I himself articulated it; 'formally rejected' is factually incorrect.
Eliminate (d): A pan-Hindu coalition formalised at Nashik is fabricated — no such agreement exists in documented history.
Confirm (a): Hindu Pad Padshahi was a rhetorical and aspirational framing of Maratha political ambition — not a formal policy with defined structures.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap here involves elevating 'Hindu Pad Padshahi' from a rhetorical aspiration to a 'formal policy.' Students who have studied Baji Rao I's northern campaigns know this phrase is associated with his vision, but the UPSC trap lies in overstating its institutional character. The concept reflected a broad political aspiration — that the Marathas should replace Mughal suzerainty with Hindu political dominance — but it was never operationalised as a formal constitutional or diplomatic policy with defined structures or binding commitments.
solution.final_explanation:
Baji Rao I articulated the vision of 'Hindu Pad Padshahi' — broadly meaning Hindu political supremacy — as a rhetorical framework for justifying Maratha expansion northward against the declining Mughal empire.

• Option (a) — Correct: It was a political and rhetorical aspiration, not a formally structured policy. Baji Rao I used it to galvanise support for northern campaigns but never codified it as an institutional programme.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Scope-extension error — calling it a 'formal policy with defined constitutional structures' vastly overstates its institutional character.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The concept was championed by the Peshwas, not formally rejected by them.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: No pan-Hindu coalition agreement was formalised at Nashik or elsewhere — this is a fabrication.

Value Addition:
• The practical reality of 'Hindu Pad Padshahi' was complicated by Maratha extraction of tribute from Rajput and other Hindu rulers — undermining any claim to a unified Hindu political programme.
• Baji Rao I's 1737 raid on Delhi demonstrated Maratha reach but also its limits — no permanent administration was established there.
• Modern historians debate whether Hindu Pad Padshahi was a genuine ideology or a post-facto rationalisation of territorial ambition.

solution.concept_anchor: Madhavrao I significance — post-Panipat revival

statement_analysis.statement: Madhavrao I undertook significant administrative and fiscal reforms after 1761 that helped rebuild the confederacy's military and financial strength in less than a decade.
statement_analysis.reason: Madhavrao I (Peshwa 1761–1772) is historically credited with rapid administrative and fiscal rehabilitation after Panipat, reasserting Maratha influence in northern India by the late 1760s — a remarkable recovery given the scale of the 1761 defeat.

statement_analysis.statement: The primary internal challenge Madhavrao I faced was managing the ambitious rivalry of Raghunathrao (Raghoba), whose repeated attempts to seize the Peshwaship destabilised the confederacy during this critical period.
statement_analysis.reason: Raghunathrao (Raghoba) — Madhavrao I's uncle — repeatedly contested Peshwa authority and sought British support for his claims, creating a persistent internal disruption that Madhavrao I had to manage while simultaneously rebuilding from Panipat.

statement_analysis.statement: Madhavrao I's significance for the Maratha Confederacy is comparable to that of Baji Rao I — both expanded Maratha territorial control to its maximum historical extent.
statement_analysis.reason: Madhavrao I's significance lies in revival and consolidation after catastrophic defeat, not territorial expansion to a maximum extent. Baji Rao I was the principal architect of territorial expansion. Equating their contributions misattributes Madhavrao I's role — he restored what had been lost rather than conquering new territory.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'all three' is deceptive for students who know Madhavrao I was genuinely important (like Baji Rao I) and may accept Statement 3's comparison without scrutinising whether 'maximum territorial expansion' is accurate for Madhavrao I.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: Madhavrao I's post-Panipat fiscal and administrative reforms are well-documented — correct.
Confirm Statement 2: Raghoba's repeated succession challenges are a defining feature of Madhavrao I's reign — correct.

Evaluate Statement 3 critically: 'Both expanded territory to maximum historical extent' — Madhavrao I's achievement was revival, not maximum expansion. Baji Rao I holds that distinction. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Correct statements are 1 and 2 only — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap here subtly equates Madhavrao I's significance with Baji Rao I's, specifically on the dimension of territorial expansion. Both Peshwas are high-yield exam figures, but for different reasons. A student who has memorised 'both were great Peshwas' without differentiating their contributions will accept Statement 3. The precise distinction: Baji Rao I = peak territorial expansion; Madhavrao I = post-Panipat revival and consolidation.
solution.final_explanation:
Madhavrao I (1745–1772) is one of the most underrated figures in Maratha history despite being arguably the most critical for the confederacy's survival. His decade-long tenure after Panipat demonstrated extraordinary administrative talent.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Within a decade of Panipat, Madhavrao I had restored the confederacy's fiscal base and reasserted Maratha influence at Delhi — a recovery few expected after the scale of the 1761 defeat.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Raghoba (Raghunathrao) was a persistent destabilising force — his ambitions culminated in British intervention and the First Anglo-Maratha War after Madhavrao I's early death in 1772.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Maximum territorial expansion belongs to the Baji Rao I era. Madhavrao I's achievement was restorative, not expansionary — a distinction UPSC specifically targets.

Value Addition:
• Madhavrao I died at only 27 years of age — his early death created the succession vacuum that Raghoba exploited.
• His short reign (1761–1772) is sometimes called the 'second golden age' of the Peshwaship.
• The Raghoba controversy directly caused British intervention — the thread from Panipat to the First Anglo-Maratha War runs through Madhavrao I's incomplete revival.

solution.concept_anchor: Differential and sequential acceptance of Subsidiary Alliance by Maratha chiefs

statement_analysis.statement: The Peshwa was the first among the major Maratha chiefs to accept the Subsidiary Alliance, doing so through the Treaty of Bassein in 1802.
statement_analysis.reason: The Treaty of Bassein (1802) made Peshwa Baji Rao II the first of the major Maratha chiefs to formally accept the Subsidiary Alliance — this is historically accurate and the statement is correct (not incorrect).

statement_analysis.statement: All five principal Maratha chief houses — Peshwa, Bhonsle, Scindia, Holkar, and Gaekwad — accepted the Subsidiary Alliance simultaneously after the Treaty of Bassein.
statement_analysis.reason: The chiefs did not accept simultaneously. The Peshwa accepted in 1802 (Bassein); Bhonsle and Scindia were compelled through the Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803); Holkars accepted last in 1818 after the Third Anglo-Maratha War — the process was sequential over 16 years.

statement_analysis.statement: The Holkars were the last among the major Maratha confederacy chiefs to formally accept the Subsidiary Alliance, doing so only after the conclusion of the Third Anglo-Maratha War in 1818.
statement_analysis.reason: The Holkars' formal acceptance of the Subsidiary Alliance came in 1818, making them the last of the major Maratha houses to be brought under the system — this statement is correct (not incorrect).

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) pointing to Statement 3 is deceptive because students who are uncertain about the exact sequencing of Holkar acceptance may doubt whether 1818 is accurate or whether it was earlier.
elimination_logic: Check Statement 1: Peshwa = first to accept via Bassein 1802 — correct, so this is NOT an incorrect statement.
Check Statement 2: 'All five accepted simultaneously after Bassein' — demonstrably false; acceptance was sequential over 1802–1818. This IS an incorrect statement.
Check Statement 3: Holkars last in 1818 — correctly stated; this is NOT an incorrect statement.
Only Statement 2 is NOT correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap exploits the assumption that a major policy like the Subsidiary Alliance would have been applied uniformly at one time. Students who know the Subsidiary Alliance eventually covered all Maratha chiefs may assume it happened at once, making Statement 2 seem plausible. The key factual precision is that acceptance was staggered over 16 years (1802–1818), with Holkars being the last holdouts.
solution.final_explanation:
Lord Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance was applied to the Maratha Confederacy in sequential stages, not simultaneously. This differential application was itself a British strategy — neutralising chiefs one by one rather than facing unified resistance.

• Statement 1 — Correct (not the incorrect one): Peshwa Baji Rao II through Bassein (1802) was first — a historically accurate claim.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The 'simultaneous' claim is false. Scindias and Bhonsles were compelled through the Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803–1805); Holkars only in 1818. The process spanned 16 years.
• Statement 3 — Correct (not the incorrect one): Holkars as last acceptors in 1818 is accurate.

Value Addition:
• The Subsidiary Alliance effectively created a British-controlled military presence inside each Maratha territory, rendering independent military action structurally impossible.
• Wellesley's genius was using the Peshwa's acceptance (Bassein) as a legal pretext to compel other chiefs.
• The sequential nature of Alliance acceptance meant each chief faced British pressure alone, unable to coordinate resistance — divide-and-rule made structural.

Statement 3 — Incorrect: Holkars did not build an equivalent European-style regular infantry — this is the false statement.
Statement 4 — Correct: Chauth and plunder as the financial basis of confederacy military power is an accurate structural characterisation.
Three statements correct (1, 2, 4); one incorrect (3) — select 'Only three', which is option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap works by extending the Scindia's European-commander model to the Holkars. Students who know that 'Maratha forces modernised under European commanders' may generalise this to all confederacy chiefs. The critical precision is that it was specifically the Scindias who developed this model — the Holkars remained more reliant on cavalry and irregular warfare, which is why their military style was fundamentally different from the Scindia regular infantry corps.
solution.final_explanation:
The Scindia military modernisation under De Boigne and Perron was the most significant European military influence on any Indian power before the Anglo-Maratha Wars. This European-trained infantry gave the Scindias a temporary battlefield advantage but ultimately proved insufficient against British forces at Assaye and Laswari.

Value Addition:
• De Boigne trained approximately 40,000 regular infantry for Mahadaji Scindia — an enormous force by contemporary Indian standards.
• The British specifically targeted De Boigne/Perron-trained forces in 1803, recognising them as the confederacy's most dangerous military asset.
• Yashwantrao Holkar's guerrilla tactics actually proved more difficult for the British to counter than the Scindia regular infantry — conventional armies are easier to defeat in pitched battle.

solution.concept_anchor: Nagpur Bhonsles vs Satara Bhonsles — two distinct lineages

statement_analysis.statement: The Bhonsles of Nagpur are a distinct dynastic line from the Bhonsles of Satara — the Nagpur branch descended from a collateral line and became a separate political entity within the Maratha Confederacy.
statement_analysis.reason: The Nagpur Bhonsles (descended from Raghuji I) were a collateral branch — not the direct Satara line of Shivaji — and functioned as a semi-independent house within the confederacy, with distinct territorial jurisdiction in Nagpur, Central India, and eastern regions.

statement_analysis.statement: Raghuji Bhonsle I expanded Maratha influence into Bengal and Orissa, making the Nagpur house primarily associated with expansion in western and coastal Maharashtra rather than eastern India.
statement_analysis.reason: Raghuji Bhonsle I's distinctive contribution was precisely his eastern expansion — into Bengal, Orissa, and Central India — not western or coastal Maharashtra. The statement reverses his geographic domain, which was emphatically eastern and central, not western.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor for students who correctly identify Statement 1 as accurate but fail to catch the geographic reversal in Statement 2, accepting 'western Maharashtra expansion' as plausible for a Bhonsle chief.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Nagpur Bhonsles as a distinct collateral line from Satara Bhonsles is historically accurate — Statement 1 is correct.

Verify Statement 2: 'Primarily associated with western and coastal Maharashtra' — this is the geographic reversal. Raghuji I's domain was eastern (Bengal, Orissa, Central India) — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — the answer is (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges the general association of 'Bhonsle = Maharashtra/western India' with the specific Nagpur branch's actual eastern expansion. Students who know the Bhonsle name from Shivaji's western Maratha context may uncritically accept that any Bhonsle house expanded in western Maharashtra. The Nagpur Bhonsles' defining characteristic was precisely the opposite — they were the confederacy's eastern expansionist force, reaching into Bengal and Orissa.
solution.final_explanation:
The Bhonsle name appears in two distinct dynastic contexts within Maratha history: the Satara branch (Shivaji's direct line, holding the Chhatrapati title) and the Nagpur branch (a collateral line that became one of the confederacy's five chief houses).

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Nagpur Bhonsles were a distinct collateral branch, not descended directly from Shivaji's line. They exercised semi-independent authority within the confederacy, often in tension with the Peshwas.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Geographic reversal. Raghuji Bhonsle I's campaigns were directed eastward — into Bengal, Orissa, and Central India. This eastern expansion was the Nagpur house's defining political contribution, not western or coastal Maharashtra.

Value Addition:
• Raghuji Bhonsle I conducted multiple raids into Bengal in the 1740s–1750s, causing significant disruption and eventually leading to British fortification of Calcutta.
• The Treaty of Deogaon (1803) brought the Nagpur Bhonsles under British subordination after the Second Anglo-Maratha War.
• Confusing the two Bhonsle branches is among the most common Maratha history errors in UPSC preparation.

solution.concept_anchor: Nana Fadnavis — statesman vs military commander
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students who know Nana Fadnavis was central to confederacy resistance against the British may conflate diplomatic leadership with military command, assuming he exercised both.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Nana Fadnavis did not command armies in the field — he was a political administrator and diplomat, not a military commander.

Eliminate (b): While Nana Fadnavis was important during the First Anglo-Maratha War period, option (b) overstates his role as 'supreme military strategist' — conflating diplomatic skill with military command.
Eliminate (d): Nana Fadnavis did not primarily champion territorial expansion — his role was defensive consolidation and diplomatic maneuvering to maintain confederacy coherence.

Confirm (c): Nana Fadnavis is historically characterised as the de facto administrator during the weak Peshwa period (Sawai Madhavrao), a skilled diplomat who maintained confederacy cohesion primarily through political skill, not military force.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges diplomatic mastery with military command. Nana Fadnavis was one of the shrewdest political operators of the late 18th century — but his power derived from administrative control and diplomatic skill, not battlefield command. Students who see 'pivotal role in confederacy resistance' may assume military leadership was involved. His death in 1800 weakened the confederacy not because a general was lost, but because the political glue binding the disparate chiefs was removed.
solution.final_explanation:
Nana Fadnavis (Nana Phadnavis) was the dominant political figure of the Maratha Confederacy in its final decades, exercising de facto administrative authority during the reign of the weak child-Peshwa Sawai Madhavrao (Madhavrao II).

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Nana Fadnavis was not a field commander — he did not lead armies in battle.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Overstates his military role. He was a diplomatic and administrative genius, not a 'supreme military strategist.'
• Option (c) — Correct: As de facto administrator during weak Peshwa rule, Nana Fadnavis maintained confederacy coherence through political skill and diplomacy. His death in 1800 removed the last effective check on inter-chief rivalries, accelerating the confederacy's fragmentation before the Second Anglo-Maratha War.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Territorial expansion was not Nana Fadnavis's primary objective — defensive consolidation and diplomatic balancing were.

Value Addition:
• Nana Fadnavis is sometimes compared to Bismarck for his skill in managing competing powers through diplomacy rather than force.
• The British recognised him as the most dangerous opponent — not because he could field armies, but because he could forge alliances they could not counter diplomatically.
• His death in 1800 — two years before the Treaty of Bassein — is seen as a turning point after which Maratha diplomatic coherence collapsed.

Decline of the Maratha Confederacy: Multi-Causal Analysis

solution.concept_anchor: Multi-causal decline — Panipat not the sole cause
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who know both A and R are factually true may hastily conclude R explains A without recognising that R provides only a partial, not complete, causal account of A.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. The Maratha Confederacy's decline resulted from a combination of structural weaknesses, British strategic advantages, and socio-economic failures — this multi-causal characterisation is historically accurate.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. The Battle of Panipat (1761) was indeed a catastrophic military defeat that killed thousands including key commanders, and the confederacy did eventually recover under Madhavrao I — both factual claims within R are accurate.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. R establishes that Panipat was severe AND that recovery was possible, which actually contradicts a monocausal explanation. A's multi-causal framing is not explained by the observation about Panipat alone — and Panipat did not produce the eventual decline; the Anglo-Maratha Wars and Subsidiary Alliance system did.
Both A and R correct but R does NOT explain A — answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap is subtle: R contains true facts (Panipat was catastrophic; recovery happened) but uses them in a way that could mislead students into thinking R explains A. In reality, A asserts multi-causality while R's framing — though factually accurate — focuses on a single event (Panipat) and its recovery, which neither captures the full causal picture nor explains the eventual terminal decline. The decline was caused by the British Subsidiary Alliance system, inter-chief rivalries, and structural weaknesses — not primarily by Panipat, from which the confederacy did recover.
solution.final_explanation:
The decline of the Maratha Confederacy is one of the richest analytical themes in UPSC Medieval History, precisely because single-cause explanations are insufficient.

Assertion (A) analysis: Correct. The confederacy's decline involved structural design flaws (decentralised command, inter-chief rivalry), British strategic superiority (Subsidiary Alliance, financial resources, divide-and-rule), and unsustainable economic models (Chauth dependency, overextension). No single event explains it.

Reason (R) analysis: Also factually correct. Panipat (1761) was genuinely catastrophic — thousands of soldiers and key commanders died. The confederacy did recover under Madhavrao I within a decade. Both observations in R are historically accurate.

Causal relationship: R does not explain A. A asserts multi-causality; R describes a single event (Panipat) and its aftermath. Furthermore, since the confederacy recovered from Panipat, Panipat itself cannot be the explanation for the terminal decline — which came later through the Anglo-Maratha Wars.

Value Addition:
• The confederacy's decline should be dated to 1817–1818 (Third Anglo-Maratha War), not to 1761 (Panipat).
• British fiscal and diplomatic superiority — not just military — was decisive in the confederacy's end.
• Single-cause answers (Panipat = decline) are specifically what UPSC constructs traps against.

solution.concept_anchor: Assaye and Argaon — Wellesley's victories against which Maratha chiefs
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students know Wellesley fought major battles during the Second Anglo-Maratha War and may conflate his opponents at different battles.
elimination_logic: Recall: Arthur Wellesley's principal campaigns in the Second Anglo-Maratha War were directed against the Scindias (Gwalior) and the Bhonsles (Nagpur) in the Deccan and Central India.
Battle of Assaye (1803): Fought against the combined forces of Scindias and Bhonsles — Wellesley later called it his most hard-fought battle.
Battle of Argaon (also 1803): Also fought against the Bhonsle forces in the context of the Deccan campaign.
Eliminate (a): Placing Assaye solely against Holkars is incorrect — Holkars were not Wellesley's primary opponents at Assaye.
Confirm (c): Assaye and Argaon were both fought by Wellesley against Scindia and Bhonsle forces — this is the correctly matched pair.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap exploits the multiple Anglo-Maratha War battles involving different chiefs. Students who know 'Wellesley fought the Marathas' but have not precision-mapped which battle was against which chief will confuse Assaye (Scindia/Bhonsle) with campaigns against Holkars. The Holkars were Lord Lake's opponents at Farrukhabad and Bharatpur — a different campaign, different commander, different opponent.
solution.final_explanation:
The Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803–1805) saw Arthur Wellesley operating in the Deccan against Scindias and Bhonsles while Lord Lake campaigned in northern India.

• Option (a) — Incorrectly matched: Assaye was not fought against the Holkars — it was fought against the combined Scindia-Bhonsle forces.
• Option (b) — Incorrectly matched: Treaty of Deogaon was with the Bhonsle, not the Scindia — this swaps the treaty signatories.
• Option (c) — Correctly matched: Both Assaye and Argaon were fought by Wellesley against the Scindia and Bhonsle forces in the Deccan — this is the accurate pairing.
• Option (d) — Incorrectly matched: Treaty of Surji-Anjangaon was with Scindia, not Holkar — again an entity-swap.

Value Addition:
• Arthur Wellesley (later Duke of Wellington) called the Battle of Assaye the 'bloodiest for the numbers engaged' of all his battles — including Waterloo.
• Lord Lake defeated the Scindia forces at the Battle of Laswari in northern India simultaneously with Wellesley's Deccan campaigns.
• The two treaties — Deogaon (Bhonsle) and Surji-Anjangaon (Scindia) — effectively neutralised the two most capable Maratha military opponents before the Third Anglo-Maratha War.

solution.concept_anchor: Peshwa constitutional subordination vs practical dominance over Chhatrapati
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students who know the Chhatrapati was the legitimate sovereign may incorrectly assume the Peshwa's authority derived from a formal constitutional amendment that elevated his status to co-sovereign.
elimination_logic: Recall the Chhatrapati-Peshwa relationship: constitutionally, the Peshwa was the chief minister of the Chhatrapati — the latter remained the nominal sovereign.
In practice, after Balaji Vishwanath secured the hereditary Peshwaship, real power shifted to the Peshwa while the Chhatrapati became ceremonial.
Eliminate (a): 'Equal co-sovereign' misrepresents the relationship — no formal co-sovereignty was ever declared.
Eliminate (c) and (d): These mischaracterise the relationship as either formally reformed or as the Peshwa being constitutionally subordinate in practice.

Confirm (b): The relationship was one of constitutional subordination (Peshwa as minister of Chhatrapati) combined with practical dominance (real power exercised by Peshwa) — the critical tension at the heart of confederacy governance.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap here exploits the confusion between formal constitutional hierarchy and actual power distribution. Students who know the Peshwa was 'below' the Chhatrapati may choose an option emphasising formal subordination without recognising that this is only the constitutional layer. The deeper truth — that practical dominance rested with the Peshwa — is the critical nuance UPSC tests.
solution.final_explanation:
The Chhatrapati-Peshwa relationship defines the constitutional paradox at the heart of the Maratha Confederacy. Nominally, the Peshwa remained the Chhatrapati's chief minister — subordinate, appointed by, and accountable to the Chhatrapati. In practice, from Balaji Vishwanath onward, the Peshwa exercised near-complete executive authority while the Chhatrapati at Satara became increasingly ceremonial.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: 'Equal co-sovereign' was never the formal or practical arrangement.
• Option (b) — Correct: Constitutional subordination (Peshwa as minister) coexisted with practical dominance (real power with Peshwa) — this dual character is the accurate description.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: No formal constitutional amendment elevated the Peshwa to co-sovereign status.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Peshwa was not constitutionally subordinate in practice — this is the exact opposite of what actually happened.

Value Addition:
• The Chhatrapati at Satara effectively became a rubber stamp — granting legitimacy to Peshwa decisions but exercising no independent authority.
• This arrangement mirrors the relationship between the Japanese Emperor and the Shogun in some respects.
• The British used the Chhatrapati's nominal sovereignty to legitimise their post-1818 settlement — installing a Chhatrapati at Satara as a managed figurehead.

solution.concept_anchor: Treaty of Salbai vs Treaty of Purandar — distinctions

statement_analysis.statement: The Convention of Wadgaon (1779) resulted in a British military defeat and required the British to restore territories acquired since 1773, making it one of the most significant early British reverses in western India.
statement_analysis.reason: The Convention of Wadgaon humiliated the British Bombay forces and required them to restore territories — it stands as one of the rare successful Maratha military confrontations with the British before the confederacy's eventual decline.

statement_analysis.statement: The Treaty of Salbai (1782) restored the pre-war territorial status quo and, by giving the British time to consolidate their position in Mysore and Bengal, proved strategically advantageous to the British in the long run.
statement_analysis.reason: The Treaty of Salbai ended the First Anglo-Maratha War on a broadly status quo basis, but by securing peace for approximately two decades it allowed the British to consolidate against Hyder Ali/Tipu Sultan in Mysore — making it a strategically advantageous outcome for the British despite its apparent balance.

statement_analysis.statement: The Treaty of Purandar (1776) permanently ended Maratha support for Raghunathrao (Raghoba) and was the definitive peace agreement that concluded the First Anglo-Maratha War.
statement_analysis.reason: The Treaty of Purandar (1776) was neither permanent nor the war's conclusion — the Marathas repudiated it, and hostilities continued until the Treaty of Salbai (1782) concluded the war. Purandar was an early and unsuccessful diplomatic attempt, not the final settlement.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'all three correct' tempts students who confidently know Statements 1 and 2 but have not carefully verified the specific claim about Purandar being the 'definitive' conclusion of the war.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: Wadgaon (1779) as a British defeat requiring territorial restoration is well-established — correct.
Confirm Statement 2: Salbai (1782) as status quo settlement strategically benefiting the British long-term is historically established — correct.

Examine Statement 3: 'Purandar permanently ended Maratha support for Raghoba AND concluded the First Anglo-Maratha War' — both claims are false. Purandar was repudiated; Salbai (not Purandar) concluded the war. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 correct; Statement 3 incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap replaces Salbai (1782) with Purandar (1776) as the war's conclusion. Students who have encountered both treaty names may conflate them, accepting that 'a treaty in the First Anglo-Maratha War period' ended the war — without precisely tracking which treaty did which. Purandar preceded the full outbreak of hostilities; Salbai ended them. The six-year gap between these two events is the temporal precision UPSC rewards.
solution.final_explanation:
The First Anglo-Maratha War generated three key agreements — the Treaty of Purandar (1776), the Convention of Wadgaon (1779), and the Treaty of Salbai (1782) — each with distinct significance.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Wadgaon was a genuine British military setback. The Bombay forces were compelled to cede recent territorial acquisitions — a moment that the Marathas celebrated and the British were anxious to reverse.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Salbai restored the pre-war status quo but gave the British breathing space to focus on the Second Anglo-Mysore War — a strategic dividend the Marathas did not foresee.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Purandar was an early, repudiated agreement — not the war's conclusion. It was rejected by the Maratha Peshwa, leading to continued hostilities and eventually Wadgaon and Salbai. Calling it 'definitive' or the 'conclusion' is precisely backward.

Value Addition:
• Mahadaji Scindia played a pivotal diplomatic role in brokering the Treaty of Salbai, enhancing his personal prestige.
• The Convention of Wadgaon is notable for being repudiated by the British Bengal government — the Bombay Presidency signed it but Calcutta refused to honour it.
• The Salbai status quo gave the confederacy its last extended period of relative peace before the Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803).

solution.concept_anchor: Evolution from guerrilla to conventional warfare under confederacy
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students know De Boigne trained Scindia forces — associating him with the Holkars rather than Scindias represents a plausible-sounding swap that requires precise knowledge to detect.
elimination_logic: Identify the category: three of the four options describe features of the Scindia military modernisation under European commanders.
Option (a): European-style disciplined infantry battalions — characterises Scindia forces under De Boigne. Belongs to Scindia modernisation.
Option (b): De Boigne as European commander — specifically associated with Scindia military organisation. Belongs to Scindia modernisation.
Option (c): Perron continuing De Boigne's infantry system — directly continues the Scindia European-commander tradition. Belongs to Scindia modernisation.
Option (d): Guerrilla cavalry raids as the primary tactical mode — this characterises Holkar (and pre-confederacy Maratha) warfare, NOT the Scindia modernised infantry model. This is the odd one out.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap assumes students will associate 'guerrilla cavalry raids' with the Maratha military tradition generally and not distinguish between houses. In fact, the Holkars maintained a cavalry-centric, irregular tactical style while the Scindias specifically shifted toward European-trained regular infantry. The question tests whether students can disaggregate the military styles of different confederacy houses rather than treating 'Maratha military' as monolithic.
solution.final_explanation:
The Scindia military modernisation represents a specific subset of confederacy military history — not a feature of all Maratha houses equally.

• Option (a) — Belongs to Scindia model: De Boigne built disciplined infantry battalions on European lines — the defining innovation of Scindia military power.
• Option (b) — Belongs to Scindia model: De Boigne himself was the European commander who created this system for Mahadaji Scindia.
• Option (c) — Belongs to Scindia model: Perron continued and expanded De Boigne's work as commander of Scindia regular forces until 1803.
• Option (d) — ODD ONE OUT: Guerrilla cavalry raids characterise the traditional Maratha tactical mode associated with Shivaji's original system and with Holkar warfare. This is emphatically NOT a feature of the European-infantry Scindia model — it is the model that the Scindia modernisation replaced.

Value Addition:
• The Holkar tactical style — light cavalry, rapid movement, avoidance of pitched battles — was actually more difficult for the British to counter than the Scindia regular infantry.
• The British Lake found Yashwantrao Holkar's guerrilla-style campaigns particularly frustrating during 1804.
• The transition from guerrilla to conventional warfare under confederacy chiefs left the Marathas vulnerable to British pitched-battle tactics.

Students who have memorised the Ashta Pradhan list without anchoring each office to its specific function will swap these two. solution.final_explanation:

Correct matches:
• A → 3 (Sardeshmukhi / hereditary claim): Sardeshmukhi was justified by the Chhatrapati's claim to be the hereditary senior headman (Sardeshmukh) of all Maharashtra — a traditional right claim, not a military protection payment.
• B → 1 (Amatya / finance): The Amatya was the finance minister responsible for revenue accounts and treasury oversight in Shivaji's administration.
• C → 4 (Sachiv / correspondence): The Sachiv (also called Shuru Navis) was keeper of royal correspondence and official records — distinct from the Sumant who handled foreign affairs and relations with external powers.
• D → 2 (Chauth / quarter-revenue protection levy): Chauth = one-fourth (25%) of assessed revenue, paid to avoid Maratha military depredation.

Value Addition:
• Sumant (foreign minister) handled relations with Mughal governors, Rajput chiefs, and other external powers — a distinction from Sachiv.
• Together Chauth + Sardeshmukhi = 35% of assessed revenue — a heavy combined burden.
• The Senapati (military commander) was arguably the most powerful Ashta Pradhan member under Shivaji's active campaigns.
