solution.concept_anchor: Panipat consequences — short-term vs long-term, military vs diplomatic

statement_analysis.statement: The Third Battle of Panipat (1761) resulted in the permanent end of Maratha political influence in northern India, from which the confederacy never recovered.
statement_analysis.reason: The 'permanent end' claim is false — Madhavrao I (Peshwa) successfully restored Maratha influence in northern India within a decade, reasserting presence at Delhi by the late 1760s. Panipat was a severe setback, not a permanent end.

statement_analysis.statement: The confederacy's diplomatic failures — including the absence of Nizam's support and the Holkars' limited participation — were significant contributing factors to the defeat at Panipat alongside the military and logistical challenges.
statement_analysis.reason: Diplomatic failures were indeed multi-dimensional contributors to Panipat — the Nizam allied against the Marathas, the Holkars did not participate effectively, and the Marathas failed to secure northern Indian allies. This is historically accurate and thus NOT an incorrect statement.

statement_analysis.statement: Ahmad Shah Durrani's Afghan forces prevailed at Panipat primarily because of their numerical superiority — the Maratha forces were significantly smaller in total strength.
statement_analysis.reason: Numerical superiority was not the primary factor — the Maratha force was substantial. The defeat resulted from logistical overstretch, supply line failure over winter, Afghan cavalry superiority in open-field battle, and political isolation, not from being numerically inferior.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) pointing to Statement 3 as the only incorrect one tempts students who correctly identify the 'permanent end' in Statement 1 as false but may believe Statement 3 is also incorrect without being certain.
elimination_logic: Check Statement 1: 'Permanent end of Maratha influence in northern India' — false, because Madhavrao I restored it within a decade. Statement 1 IS incorrect.
Check Statement 2: Diplomatic failures including Nizam and Holkar non-cooperation as contributing factors — this is historically accurate. Statement 2 is NOT incorrect.

Check Statement 3: 'Prevailed primarily because of numerical superiority' — the Marathas were not significantly numerically inferior; defeat was due to logistics and tactics. Statement 3 IS incorrect.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 1 adds 'permanent' to what would otherwise be a true statement (Panipat was a severe blow to Maratha northern influence). The word 'permanent' converts a true claim into a false one because the confederacy did recover. Students who accept the severity of Panipat without recalling the post-Panipat Madhavrao I revival will miss this. Statement 3 similarly extends 'numerical' as the primary factor beyond what historical evidence supports.
solution.final_explanation:
Panipat (1761) was catastrophic but not terminal — and the causes of defeat were multi-dimensional, not monocausal.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The 'permanent end' qualifier is factually wrong. Madhavrao I restored Maratha influence at Delhi within less than a decade — the recovery is documented. Panipat was severe, not permanent.
• Statement 2 — Correct (not the incorrect one): Diplomatic isolation — Nizam against the Marathas, Holkar limited participation — was a genuine multi-dimensional contributor to defeat alongside logistics and tactics.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Marathas were not decisively numerically inferior at Panipat. The defeat resulted from supply line disruption over a winter siege, Afghan cavalry superiority in the open battle, and political isolation from potential northern allies — not from raw numbers.

Value Addition:
• The Maratha force at Panipat included approximately 45,000–60,000 fighting men plus an enormous non-combatant camp — logistics, not numbers, was the fatal weakness.
• Madhavrao I's reassertion at Delhi occurred by approximately 1771 — just a decade after Panipat.
• Ahmad Shah Durrani himself withdrew to Afghanistan after Panipat and never returned — the Afghan victory did not translate into permanent Afghan control of northern India either.

solution.concept_anchor: Holkar vs Scindia rivalry — Battle of Ujjain origins
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students who know there was a Scindia-Holkar rivalry may confuse its origins (Battle of Ujjain, 1728) with the Battle of Panipat or other named conflicts.
elimination_logic: Recall: The Holkar-Scindia rivalry is among the most consequential inter-confederacy conflicts.
The Battle of Ujjain (1728) is the specific early conflict marking the origins of Holkar-Scindia tensions — not any later battle.
Eliminate (b): Battle of Wadgaon is associated with the First Anglo-Maratha War (British defeat), not inter-Maratha conflict.
Eliminate (c): Battle of Panipat involved the Afghan-Maratha conflict, not Holkar-Scindia rivalry specifically.
Eliminate (d): Battle of Assaye was fought between the British and Scindia/Bhonsle forces in 1803.
Confirm (a): The Battle of Ujjain (1728) marks the documented origins of the Holkar-Scindia competition for dominance in Malwa.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap exploits students who know 'there was a battle' associated with Holkar-Scindia tensions but swap the specific battle name. The Battle of Ujjain (1728) is the precise origin point — early in the confederacy's history. Students who have not specifically anchored this battle to the Holkar-Scindia rivalry will default to more famous battles (Panipat, Wadgaon) that have no connection to this inter-house conflict.
solution.final_explanation:
Inter-house rivalry within the Maratha Confederacy was a structural feature, not an anomaly. The Holkar-Scindia conflict was the most persistent and consequential of these rivalries.

• Option (a) — Correct: The Battle of Ujjain (1728) marks the early origins of Holkar-Scindia competition for control over the Malwa region — both houses had territorial interests there and the conflict began within a decade of the confederacy's institutional formation.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The Convention of Wadgaon (1779) was a British-Maratha event, not an inter-house conflict.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Third Battle of Panipat (1761) was an Afghan-Maratha conflict. While Holkar non-participation weakened the Maratha cause, the battle itself was not a Holkar-Scindia confrontation.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Battle of Assaye (1803) was fought between the British and the combined Scindia-Bhonsle forces.

Value Addition:
• Holkar-Scindia rivalry was exploited by the British to prevent unified Maratha resistance — each house feared the other gaining British favour.
• Yashwantrao Holkar defeated Peshwa Baji Rao II at the Battle of Hadapsar (1802) — indirectly causing the Treaty of Bassein.
• The Peshwas were unable to permanently arbitrate Holkar-Scindia disputes, reflecting the confederacy's structural inability to enforce collective discipline.

solution.concept_anchor: Subsidiary Alliance structural dismantlement of Maratha military independence
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because inter-chief rivalry is a genuine cause of Maratha decline, and students who have studied internal fragmentation may select it without recognising that the scenario specifically describes the structural effect of the Subsidiary Alliance.
elimination_logic: Read the scenario: A major power deploys its troops inside a subordinate ally's territory; the subordinate pays for these troops; the subordinate cannot maintain independent external relations. This precisely describes the Subsidiary Alliance mechanism.

Identify the structural consequence the question asks about: 'rendered collective military resistance structurally impossible before any war began' — this requires identifying the pre-conflict neutralisation mechanism.
Eliminate (a): Doctrine of Paramountcy is a later formalisation of British supremacy — not the mechanism described in the scenario.
Eliminate (c): Inter-chief rivalry is a real factor but is not what the scenario describes — the scenario focuses on a structural-military mechanism imposed by an external power.
Eliminate (d): Forward Policy (Dalhousie) is unrelated to the confederacy period.

Confirm (b): The Subsidiary Alliance precisely describes the mechanism — troops stationed inside, costs borne by the ally, foreign policy controlled by the British — which structurally dismantled military independence before open conflict.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap in option (c) exploits the fact that inter-chief rivalry was a genuine cause of Maratha decline — making it feel like a correct answer. But the scenario specifically describes an externally imposed structural mechanism (British troops inside Maratha territories, paid by Maratha funds, with controlled foreign policy) — which is the Subsidiary Alliance, not internal rivalry. Students who read the scenario too quickly will anchor to 'rivalries prevented unified response' rather than the structural mechanism being described.
solution.final_explanation:
Lord Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance was one of the most ingenious strategic instruments of British Indian expansion. By stationing troops inside an ally's territory at the ally's expense, the British achieved three objectives simultaneously: they controlled the ally's foreign policy, drained the ally's treasury, and maintained a military presence that could be activated against the ally if needed.

How the scenario maps to the Subsidiary Alliance:
• British troops stationed inside Maratha territories — paid for by the Maratha chief's own revenue — created a structural military presence that made independent Maratha military action dangerous.
• Control over foreign relations meant no Maratha chief could forge anti-British alliances without British knowledge and intervention.
• The mechanism worked before any battle was fought — the confederacy's military independence was structurally dismantled through paper agreements, not conquest.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Doctrine of Paramountcy is a later framework, not the structural mechanism described.
• Option (b) — Correct: The Subsidiary Alliance precisely fits every element of the scenario.
• Option (c) — Incorrect (partial truth): Inter-chief rivalry was a real factor but is not what the scenario's specific structural elements describe.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Forward Policy is from the Dalhousie era, irrelevant here.

Value Addition:
• The Subsidiary Alliance effectively made each accepting Maratha chief financially dependent on continued British cooperation — resistance became economically irrational.
• Wellesley applied the Alliance to Hyderabad (1798) and Mysore (1799) before targeting the Marathas.
• The genius of the Alliance was that it was accepted voluntarily — usually under duress, but without direct conquest.

The costs of maintaining these contingents were borne entirely by the respective chief from his own revenue. A historian observes that this arrangement rendered collective military resistance by the confederation structurally impossible before any formal war had begun.

(d) The Forward Policy of the Governor-General, which required the pre-emptive annexation of buffer territories before they could be used against British interests

solution.concept_anchor: Peshwa office — chronological evolution from minister to hereditary power
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because students who know Balaji Vishwanath preceded Baji Rao I may accept a sequence that reverses the Shahu-Balaji Vishwanath political alliance and the Battle of Khed.
elimination_logic: The Battle of Khed (1707): First event — Balaji Vishwanath helped Shahu defeat Tarabai, establishing the political basis for the Peshwa's rise. This must come first.
Shahu granting hereditary Peshwaship to Balaji Vishwanath: This flows directly from Khed — Balaji Vishwanath's reward for political service, establishing the hereditary Peshwaship.
Baji Rao I becoming Peshwa (1720) and launching northern campaigns: He succeeded his father Balaji Vishwanath — this must come after the hereditary grant.
Balaji Baji Rao (Nana Saheb) becoming Peshwa (1740): He succeeded Baji Rao I — this is the final event. Sequence: Khed → Hereditary grant → Baji Rao I → Balaji Baji Rao. Select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap involves placing Baji Rao I before the hereditary grant to Balaji Vishwanath, or placing the Battle of Khed after the hereditary grant. Students who know these are connected events but are uncertain about the precise sequence may reverse the order. The Battle of Khed (1707) is the political precondition for all subsequent Peshwa developments — it must anchor the sequence as Event 1.
solution.final_explanation:
The evolution of the Peshwa office followed a precise causal chain — each step enabled the next.

Correct sequence:
1. Battle of Khed (1707): Balaji Vishwanath's military and political support helped Shahu (Chhatrapati) defeat his rival Tarabai — establishing his indispensability to Shahu.
2. Shahu grants hereditary Peshwaship to Balaji Vishwanath: The reward for Khed — transforming the Peshwa from an appointed post to a dynastic office, the structural foundation of confederacy governance.
3. Baji Rao I becomes Peshwa (1720): Succeeds his father; launches the northern expansion campaigns, reaching the territorial peak of Maratha power.
4. Balaji Baji Rao (Nana Saheb) becomes Peshwa (1740): Succeeds Baji Rao I; presides over both administrative refinement and eventual overextension culminating in Panipat.

Why wrong options fail: Any sequence placing Baji Rao I before the hereditary grant contradicts the causal chain — Baji Rao I's succession is only possible because his father secured the hereditary office.

Value Addition:
• The entire hereditary Peshwa line spans 1713–1818 — just over a century.
• Baji Rao I was reportedly 20 years old when he became Peshwa — one of history's youngest great commanders.
• The line ends with Baji Rao II's pensioning at Bithur in 1818 — the bookend to Balaji Vishwanath's founding moment.

solution.concept_anchor: Maratha-northern powers — tribute extraction vs genuine alliance

statement_analysis.statement: Maratha relations with Rajput states were primarily those of coercive suzerainty and tribute extraction rather than a voluntary anti-Mughal alliance based on shared political goals.
statement_analysis.reason: The Marathas extracted heavy tribute from Rajput states — Jaipur, Jodhpur, and others — often through military pressure. This was not a voluntary pan-Hindu alliance but an economic relationship of Maratha dominance, which generated resentment rather than solidarity.

statement_analysis.statement: The Marathas and Jat rulers around the Delhi-Doab region occasionally cooperated tactically, including during pre-Panipat operations, making the Maratha-Jat relationship uniformly antagonistic throughout the 18th century.
statement_analysis.reason: The statement contradicts itself — acknowledging tactical cooperation while calling the relationship 'uniformly antagonistic.' Maratha-Jat relations included periods of both cooperation and conflict; calling them 'uniformly antagonistic' is factually inaccurate.

statement_analysis.statement: One reason the Marathas failed to forge a sustained anti-British coalition with Rajput and Sikh powers was that Maratha behaviour toward both — as tribute extractors and territorial competitors — had generated lasting resentment rather than genuine alliance sentiment.
statement_analysis.reason: The Marathas' extractive approach to northern Indian powers (tribute demands, plunder, territorial pressure) made a voluntary anti-British coalition politically impossible — potential allies had more to fear from Maratha dominance than from the more distant British threat in many cases.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'all three' is itself the strong distractor — students who identify Statements 1 and 3 as correct may accept Statement 2 without catching the 'uniformly antagonistic' qualifier that makes it false.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: Coercive suzerainty and tribute extraction characterise Maratha-Rajput relations more accurately than voluntary alliance — correct.

Examine Statement 2 carefully: 'Occasionally cooperated... making the relationship uniformly antagonistic' — the presence of 'occasionally cooperated' contradicts 'uniformly antagonistic.' The 'uniformly' qualifier makes this false.
Confirm Statement 3: Resentment generated by Maratha tribute extraction prevented genuine coalition-building — historically accurate.
Statements 1 and 3 correct; Statement 2 incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 2 works through the word 'uniformly' — a qualifier that converts a partly true observation into a false one. Students who identify that Marathas and Jats had 'mostly conflicted' may accept 'uniformly antagonistic' without registering that the statement itself acknowledges cooperation ('occasionally cooperated'). This internal self-contradiction within Statement 2 is the precision test.
solution.final_explanation:
Maratha relations with northern powers were complex and cannot be reduced to either uniform alliance or uniform antagonism.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Rajput states paid tribute to the Marathas under coercive pressure — not from voluntary alliance. The Marathas' extractive posture with Rajput chiefs contrasted sharply with any pan-Hindu solidarity rhetoric.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The statement is internally contradictory — acknowledging tactical Maratha-Jat cooperation while concluding the relationship was 'uniformly antagonistic.' Jat ruler Suraj Mal had documented tactical interactions with Maratha commanders. 'Uniformly' is the killer qualifier.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The pattern of Maratha tribute extraction and territorial competition with Rajputs and Sikhs made genuine coalition-building against the British politically impossible — each potential ally calculated that Maratha dominance posed a more immediate threat than British expansion.

Value Addition:
• Suraj Mal (Jat ruler of Bharatpur) warned the Marathas about logistical vulnerabilities before Panipat — a piece of advice that was not heeded.
• Rajput chiefs often preferred British paramountcy to Maratha tribute demands — this shaped their neutrality during the Anglo-Maratha Wars.
• The failure of pan-Indian coalitions against the British was as much due to Indian inter-power rivalries as to British military superiority.

solution.concept_anchor: Second Anglo-Maratha War — Bassein as trigger via confederacy sovereignty
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) tempts students who correctly identify both A and R as true but overanalyse the causal sufficiency of R, missing that R in this case does directly and causally explain A.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. The Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803–1805) was triggered by the Scindias and Bhonsles opposing the Treaty of Bassein — this is historically established.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. Peshwa Baji Rao II accepted the Subsidiary Alliance through Bassein, surrendering control over the confederacy's foreign policy to the British — this is factually accurate.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — Yes. The Scindia and Bhonsle resistance was directly provoked by Bassein because the Peshwa's acceptance was interpreted as surrendering the entire confederacy's sovereign independence. R directly explains why other chiefs went to war. This is option (a).
Confirm: A correct + R correct + R explains A = option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation temptation here is subtle — option (b) appeals to students who have practised the 'both true but unrelated' pattern and apply it reflexively. In this question, R genuinely explains A — the Scindia-Bhonsle opposition to the Second Anglo-Maratha War was directly caused by their interpretation of Bassein as a surrender of confederacy sovereignty. Students who automatically question causal sufficiency of R may over-apply the pattern and select (b) incorrectly.
solution.final_explanation:
The Treaty of Bassein (1802) was the direct proximate cause of the Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803–1805).

Assertion (A) analysis: Correct. Daulat Rao Scindia and Raghuji Bhonsle II both opposed the Treaty of Bassein and refused to recognise its authority over the confederacy. This opposition led to British military campaigns against them — constituting the Second Anglo-Maratha War.

Reason (R) analysis: Also correct. Peshwa Baji Rao II at Bassein accepted: permanent British troops in his territories at his expense, British control over his external relations, and territorial concessions. These are the precise terms of the Subsidiary Alliance.

Causal link: R directly explains A. The Scindia and Bhonsle opposition arose precisely because Bassein transferred sovereign foreign policy control from the confederacy to the British. Other chiefs viewed this as the Peshwa unilaterally surrendering the collective confederacy's independence — a direct provocation requiring military response. R is not merely correlated with A; it causally explains it.

Value Addition:
• The Second Anglo-Maratha War ended with Treaties of Deogaon (Bhonsle, 1803) and Surji-Anjangaon (Scindia, 1803) — both involving significant territorial losses.
• Arthur Wellesley's victory at Assaye (1803) was achieved against a numerically superior force — it became the template for British Deccan campaigns.
• After Bassein and the Second Anglo-Maratha War, only the Holkars remained as a militarily independent Maratha force — until 1818.

solution.concept_anchor: Dual administrative layers — Peshwa central vs chief house autonomous administration

statement_analysis.statement: Under the Maratha Confederacy, the Peshwa maintained a central administration at Pune while each of the five principal chief houses simultaneously exercised autonomous administrative authority within their respective territorial jurisdictions.
statement_analysis.reason: The confederacy operated on a dual-layer model — Peshwa's central administration coexisted with the near-sovereign autonomous administrations of the five chief houses, each managing revenue, justice, and military matters independently in their domains.

statement_analysis.statement: The revenue systems of the individual confederacy chiefs were uniform replications of Shivaji's original administrative model, with no significant modification.
statement_analysis.reason: The individual chiefs modified and adapted revenue systems to their regional contexts — the Scindias in Gwalior, Holkars in Malwa, and Gaekwads in Gujarat each developed administrative practices reflecting local conditions rather than uniformly replicating Shivaji's Deccan-centric model.

statement_analysis.statement: A structural weakness of the confederacy's administrative design was the absence of a binding mechanism to enforce collective fiscal or military decisions across all chief houses.
statement_analysis.reason: The confederacy lacked any institutional mechanism — court, council, or treaty — that could compel all chief houses to contribute uniformly to collective military or fiscal decisions. This structural gap meant collective action depended on voluntary cooperation, which was frequently absent.

statement_analysis.statement: The Peshwa's administrative authority over the chief houses was exercised through the Ashta Pradhan, which served as a federal council overseeing both Peshwa and chief house administration.
statement_analysis.reason: The Ashta Pradhan was a ministerial council under the Chhatrapati (and later effectively under the Peshwa), not a federal council that oversaw the chief houses. The chief houses maintained autonomous administrations not subordinate to the Ashta Pradhan.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) 'Only two' tempts students who correctly identify Statements 2 and 4 as false but are uncertain about whether Statement 3's 'absence of binding mechanism' is too strong a claim.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 — Correct: Dual-layer administration (Peshwa central + chief house autonomous) is the defining administrative feature of the confederacy.
Statement 2 — Incorrect: Chief houses adapted revenue systems to regional contexts — there was no uniform replication of Shivaji's model.
Statement 3 — Correct: No binding enforcement mechanism for collective decisions is a documented structural weakness — historically supported.
Statement 4 — Incorrect: The Ashta Pradhan was not a federal council overseeing chief houses — it was the Peshwa's/Chhatrapati's ministerial body.

Two correct (1 and 3), two incorrect (2 and 4) — 'Only two' correct. Select option (b)... wait — re-examine: the question asks 'how many are correct' — Statements 1 and 3 are correct = two correct = 'Only two' = option (b). But options are (a) Only one, (b) Only two, (c) Only three, (d) All four. Two correct = option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap in Statement 4 presents the Ashta Pradhan's role in language that sounds administratively plausible — 'federal council overseeing both Peshwa and chief house administration.' Students who know the Ashta Pradhan was an important institution may accept this characterisation without recognising it was a ministerial advisory body, not a federal oversight mechanism. The word 'federal council' is the fabricated elevation of the Ashta Pradhan's actual, more limited role.
solution.final_explanation:
The confederacy's administrative structure was defined by its dual-layer design and by the absence of institutional mechanisms to enforce collective decisions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Peshwa's Pune administration and the autonomous chief house administrations coexisted — the defining feature of confederacy governance.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Revenue systems varied by region and chief. The Scindias in northern India, Holkars in Malwa, and Gaekwads in Gujarat each adapted to local conditions rather than uniformly replicating the Deccan-centric Shivaji model.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The confederacy had no binding federal enforcement mechanism. Collective military campaigns (like Panipat) depended on voluntary cooperation — and when cooperation failed (Holkar at Panipat), there was no institutional recourse.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: The Ashta Pradhan was a ministerial council of the Chhatrapati/Peshwa — not a federal council supervising the autonomous chief houses. The chief houses did not report to or receive directives from the Ashta Pradhan.

Value Addition:
• The confederacy's administrative weakness mirrors the structural problems of the Holy Roman Empire in Europe — nominal unity, practical fragmentation.
• The British exploited the absence of a binding mechanism by dealing with each chief separately, preventing collective responses.
• Revenue system diversity meant the confederacy could not maintain a centralised fiscal account — contributing to financial fragmentation.

solution.concept_anchor: Third Anglo-Maratha War — consequences and which chiefs survived

statement_analysis.statement: The Third Anglo-Maratha War ended with the abolition of the hereditary Peshwaship, the annexation of Peshwa territories, and the pensioning of Baji Rao II at Bithur near Kanpur.
statement_analysis.reason: These are the precise consequences: the Peshwaship was abolished in 1818, Peshwa territories became British-administered provinces, and Baji Rao II received a pension and residence at Bithur (not Satara or Pune) — all accurately stated.

statement_analysis.statement: Following the Third Anglo-Maratha War, the Bhonsle of Nagpur was the only Maratha chief house that retained full internal sovereignty without accepting any British oversight, in recognition of their non-participation in hostilities.
statement_analysis.reason: The Nagpur Bhonsles did participate in the Third Anglo-Maratha War (fighting the British at Nagpur) and did not retain full sovereignty — they were brought under British paramountcy. The Gaekwad of Baroda, who largely avoided active opposition, retained their position under British paramountcy, but no Maratha house retained 'full internal sovereignty' after 1818.

statement_analysis.statement: The Gaekwad of Baroda's survival as a princely state after 1818 was partly because this house had not actively opposed the British during the Third Anglo-Maratha War, unlike the Peshwa, Bhonsle, and Holkar.
statement_analysis.reason: The Gaekwads had earlier cooperated with the British and did not mount active military resistance in 1817–18, which is why Baroda survived as a princely state under British paramountcy throughout the colonial period — a direct consequence of non-confrontation.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'all three' is a strong distractor for students who have not carefully verified Statement 2's 'full internal sovereignty' claim, which is too strong — all surviving Maratha chiefs operated under British paramountcy after 1818.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: Abolition of Peshwaship, territorial annexation, Baji Rao II at Bithur — all specific facts are correctly stated. Statement 1 is correct.

Examine Statement 2: 'Bhonsle retained full internal sovereignty due to non-participation' — Nagpur Bhonsles DID fight the British in the Third Anglo-Maratha War; they did not retain full sovereignty. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Confirm Statement 3: Gaekwad non-confrontation → survival as princely state — this is the key UPSC trap dimension confirmed as correct. Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct; Statement 2 incorrect — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap in Statement 2 substitutes the Bhonsle for the Gaekwad as the non-participating house. Students who know 'one Maratha house survived more intact because they didn't fight' may accept the Bhonsle's name without checking whether it was actually the Gaekwad. The Nagpur Bhonsles actively fought the British at Nagpur in 1817 — the precise opposite of what Statement 2 claims. The Gaekwad of Baroda is the house that correctly belongs in Statement 2's description.
solution.final_explanation:
The Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817–1818) conclusively ended the Maratha Confederacy as a political entity, but its consequences varied by chief house.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Baji Rao II was pensioned at Bithur (Kanpur) — a specific geographic fact that UPSC has tested. The Peshwaship was abolished, territories annexed — all accurately stated.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Nagpur Bhonsles fought the British at Nagpur in 1817. They were brought under British paramountcy — not given 'full internal sovereignty.' The non-confrontational house was the Gaekwad of Baroda, not the Bhonsle. The 'full sovereignty' claim is also too strong — all surviving Maratha states became British-paramountcy states.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Gaekwad non-participation in active hostilities → survival of Baroda state. This is the key UPSC dimension — understanding why some chiefs survived while others were dissolved.

Value Addition:
• Baji Rao II's adopted son Nana Saheb (Dhondu Pant) became a significant figure in the 1857 uprising — the Bithur connection gives the Third Anglo-Maratha War a direct thread to 1857.
• Satara was briefly revived as a Chhatrapati-headed state under British patronage, but later annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse in 1848.
• The Holkar of Indore and Scindia of Gwalior also survived as princely states under British paramountcy — they did not cease to exist but lost all real sovereignty.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because it correctly maps Mahadaji Scindia to Delhi/Shah Alam but swaps Nana Fadnavis and Madhavrao I in ways that partially resemble the correct answer.
elimination_logic: Anchor A: Mahadaji Scindia — rehabilitated Maratha prestige after Panipat, established protectorate over Shah Alam II at Delhi. This maps to description 4.
Anchor B: Nana Fadnavis — de facto administrator during Sawai Madhavrao's reign; primarily a statesman, not a military commander. This maps to description 2.
Anchor C: Madhavrao I — post-Panipat revival through fiscal/administrative reform and military reassertion at Delhi. This maps to description 1.

Anchor D: Daulat Rao Scindia — presided over Scindia decline; defeated at Assaye and Laswari under the Second Anglo-Maratha War. This maps to description 3. Full match: A-4, B-2, C-1, D-3 = option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap here swaps the descriptions of Madhavrao I and Mahadaji Scindia — both are associated with 'Maratha revival after Panipat' and 'reassertion at Delhi.' Students who have not precisely mapped which figure achieved what may confuse them. Madhavrao I = administrative/fiscal revival (1761–1772); Mahadaji Scindia = Delhi protectorate and diplomatic rehabilitation (1770s–1794). The temporal and thematic distinction is the precision test.
solution.final_explanation:
The late 18th century Maratha political landscape was shaped by four pivotal figures with distinct roles.

Correct matches:
• A → 4 (Mahadaji Scindia / Delhi protectorate): Mahadaji Scindia exercised a formal protectorate over the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II, symbolising the restoration of Maratha influence in northern India at its most dramatic.
• B → 2 (Nana Fadnavis / diplomatic statesman): Nana Fadnavis was the political administrator during the child-Peshwa Sawai Madhavrao's reign — his death in 1800 removed the last coherent diplomatic force holding the confederacy together.
• C → 1 (Madhavrao I / post-Panipat administrative revival): Madhavrao I rebuilt the confederacy's fiscal and administrative machinery after the catastrophic 1761 defeat, reasserting Maratha presence at Delhi by the late 1760s.
• D → 3 (Daulat Rao Scindia / Second Anglo-Maratha War decline): Daulat Rao presided over Scindia's military defeats at Assaye and Laswari (1803) — the nadir of Scindia power, in sharp contrast to the Mahadaji zenith.

Value Addition:
• Mahadaji Scindia (d. 1794) and Nana Fadnavis (d. 1800) died within six years of each other — their deaths removed the two most capable leaders before the decisive Anglo-Maratha confrontations.
• Madhavrao I's reign (1761–1772) lasted only 11 years — yet is regarded as the second peak of Peshwa authority.
• Daulat Rao Scindia survived the Second Anglo-Maratha War and continued under British paramountcy until 1827.

solution.concept_anchor: Multi-causal confederacy decline — structural, British, and economic factors

statement_analysis.statement: The decentralised structure of the Maratha Confederacy — which allowed each chief house to maintain autonomous military and administrative systems — contributed to its vulnerability by preventing a unified command in collective military emergencies.
statement_analysis.reason: The confederacy's structural decentralisation was a genuine weakness — the absence of a unified command structure meant military responses to British pressure were fragmented, with each chief calculating individual interests rather than collective survival. This statement is correct.

statement_analysis.statement: British financial resources and the Subsidiary Alliance system gave the British a decisive structural advantage over the Marathas by draining Maratha revenues while simultaneously maintaining a standing British military presence inside Maratha territories.
statement_analysis.reason: The Subsidiary Alliance's genius was that it weaponised the ally's own revenue against them — Maratha funds paid for the British troops stationed within Maratha territories, draining resources while the military balance shifted decisively toward the British.

statement_analysis.statement: The Maratha Confederacy's revenue model, based primarily on Chauth and Sardeshmukhi collection, was sustainable in the long run because these levies did not require direct territorial administration and thus reduced governance costs significantly.
statement_analysis.reason: The Chauth-Sardeshmukhi model was structurally unsustainable — it depended on military reach to compel payment, meaning any territorial setback immediately reduced revenue. It also generated resentment among paying territories, making them potential British allies. The claim of long-term sustainability is the false element.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because Statement 1 contains the kind of critical analysis of confederacy weaknesses that sounds like it could be an 'incorrect' statement — students who apply a contrarian reading may mistakenly flag it as NOT correct.
elimination_logic: Check Statement 1: Decentralised structure → no unified command → vulnerability — this is accurate historical analysis. Statement 1 is correct (not the incorrect one).
Check Statement 2: British Subsidiary Alliance draining Maratha revenue while stationing troops inside — structurally accurate. Statement 2 is correct (not the incorrect one).

Check Statement 3: 'Sustainable in the long run because it reduced governance costs' — Chauth was UNSUSTAINABLE because it required military reach; any territorial loss collapsed collection. The 'sustainable' claim is false. Statement 3 IS NOT correct.
Only Statement 3 is NOT correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap in Statement 3 takes a real observation (Chauth didn't require direct administration) and converts it into a false conclusion (therefore sustainable). Students who correctly identify that Chauth avoided administrative costs may accept the 'sustainable' conclusion without recognising the deeper structural problem: sustainability required continuous military reach, which the confederacy could not maintain as British power grew. The partial truth (reduced governance costs) masks the fatal flaw (dependency on military coercion for collection).
solution.final_explanation:
The decline of the Maratha Confederacy resulted from an interaction of structural design flaws, British strategic advantages, and an unsustainable economic model — no single factor is sufficient.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Decentralised structure = no unified command = fragmented military response. Each chief weighed individual survival against collective resistance, and individual calculation consistently won — as seen in Holkar non-participation at Panipat and Gaekwad accommodation with the British.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Subsidiary Alliance was a fiscal weapon. Maratha revenues paid for the British garrison; the British garrison neutralised Maratha military independence; neutralised military independence prevented resistance. A self-reinforcing cycle of subordination.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Chauth model was not sustainable. Its revenue flow depended on the credible threat of Maratha military depredation — remove the military reach (through British-imposed treaties), and collection collapsed. It also created precisely the resentment among subjected territories that made them receptive to British protection as an alternative.

Value Addition:
• The Maratha revenue model's unsustainability is evidenced by the confederacy's chronic inability to fund coordinated campaigns without plunder income.
• The British model — territorial revenue from permanently administered lands — was far more stable than the Maratha tribute-extraction model.
• Multi-causal analysis of decline (not 'Panipat = decline') is the UPSC-preferred framework.

solution.concept_anchor: Maratha northward expansion — key campaigns and battles in sequence
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) places Baji Rao I's Delhi raid after Panipat, which some students who confuse the timing of the raid (1737) with later events may accept.
elimination_logic: Baji Rao I becomes Peshwa (1720): Start of the expansion era — must be first.
Maratha campaigns in Malwa and Gujarat (early 1720s–1730s): These preceded the Delhi raid — campaigns built the base for the audacious 1737 strike.
Baji Rao I's raid on Delhi (1737): Dramatic peak of his northern expansion — must come after Malwa/Gujarat consolidation.

Third Battle of Panipat (1761): Post-dates all Baji Rao I events by 21–41 years — must be last. Correct sequence: Baji Rao I becomes Peshwa → Malwa/Gujarat campaigns → Delhi raid → Panipat. Select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap involves placing the Malwa campaigns after the Delhi raid (reversing the logical buildup sequence) or placing Panipat before the Delhi raid. Students who memorise individual events without their causal chain may not register that the Delhi raid (1737) was the culmination of Malwa-Gujarat consolidation, not a standalone adventure. Panipat (1761) — 24 years after the Delhi raid — is unambiguously last.
solution.final_explanation:
Baji Rao I's northern expansion followed a logical strategic sequence — consolidating nearer territories before striking at the Mughal capital.

Correct sequence:
1. Baji Rao I assumes Peshwaship (1720): Launches the expansion era with his famous argument to Shahu about attacking the 'trunk' (Delhi) rather than the 'branches' of Mughal power.
2. Campaigns in Malwa and Gujarat (1720s–1730s): Systematic expansion into the resource-rich Malwa plateau and Gujarat, building the military and fiscal base for northern operations.
3. Raid on Delhi (1737): The audacious culmination — Maratha forces reached the outskirts of Delhi, demonstrating the empire's vulnerability. Baji Rao I did not capture Delhi permanently — this was a demonstration strike.
4. Third Battle of Panipat (1761): A generation later, the consequences of Maratha overextension into northern India culminated in catastrophic defeat against Ahmad Shah Durrani.

Why wrong options fail: Options placing the Delhi raid before Malwa campaigns misread the strategic sequencing; options placing Panipat before 1737 violate basic chronology.

Value Addition:
• The 1737 Delhi raid forced the Mughal Emperor Muhammad Shah to grant Malwa formally to the Marathas — a major territorial acquisition.
• Baji Rao I died in 1740, three years after the Delhi raid — he never saw Panipat.
• The Panipat disaster was partly caused by overextension that Baji Rao I's own success had made possible.
